source_text:
Μωσέως σκιαῖς, ἵνα τὴν ἐν αὐταῖς ζη τῶμεν ἀλήθειαν, καινὰ καὶ παλαιὰ ἐκ
θησαυροῦ ἐκ βάλλοντες. Εἰ δὲ βούλει, ἅπερ ἐνταῦθα συλλέξομεν ἐν παρασκευῇ,
ταῦτα ἐκεῖσε σαββατίσαντες εὑρήσο μεν καὶ τραφησόμεθα. Πάλαι μὲν οὖν ἄρτον ἀπ'
οὐρανοῦ ἔδωκεν ὁ Θεὸς τῷ λαῷ αὐτοῦ, ἀκοπιάστως πρὸς πᾶσαν ἡδονὴν ἰσχύοντα·
πρὸς ὃ γάρ τις ἐβούλετο μετε κρίνατο. Τοιαύτη δὲ ἡ τοῦ τρέφοντος τὴν ψυχὴν λό
γου φύσις, πρὸς τὴν δύναμιν τοῦ τρεφομένου μετα βάλλουσα. Ἐὰν νήπιον τρέφῃ ὁ
νόμος, γάλα γίνεται· ἐὰν ψυχὴν ἀσθενοῦσαν, λάχανον· ἐὰν τέλειον, στε ρεὰ τροφή.
Οὐ καθεζομένοις δὲ ἡμῖν ἔρχεται τὸ μάννα, ἀλλ' ἐρχομένοις ἔξω τῆς παρεμβολῆς·
λέγω δὴ τοῦ σώματος, ἐν ᾧ ἐνεῖρκται ἡ ψυχή. ∆εῖ γὰρ τὴν ψυχὴν μηκέτ' εἶναι ἐν
σαρκὶ, ἀλλ' ἐν πνεύματι. Οὐδεὶς δὲ, φορῶν τὴν εἰκόνα τοῦ χοϊκοῦ, δύναται ἄρτον
οὐράνιον φαγεῖν· διότι ψυχικὸς ἄνθρωπος 17.145 οὐ δέχεται τὰ τοῦ πνεύματος. Περὶ
ἧς τροφῆς καὶ σὺ ἐδιδάχθης εὔχεσθαι. Ἐὰν οὖν τὸν ἐπιούσιον ἄρτον, τὸν μὴ
ἐκχωροῦντα, τὸν μὴ ἀποκρινόμενον, τὸν ἀναδιδόμενον εἰς τὴν οὐσίαν τῆς ψυχῆς,
ὅταν διαλαμβάνω περὶ Θεοῦ, περὶ Χριστοῦ, περὶ τῆς θεότητος αὐτοῦ, περὶ τῆς ἐν
ἀνθρωπίνῳ σώματι καὶ ψυχῇ αὐτοῦ ἐνοικήσεως, ἄρτον ἀγγέλων ἐσθίω, τὸ μάννα·
ὅπερ εὑρὼν καὶ θαυμάσας, θαυμαστικῶς ἐρῶ· Μάν; τί ἐστι τοῦτο; καὶ γενήσεται
τοῦτο τὸ φθέγμα τῷ ἄρτῳ ὄνομα· εὔξασθε ἵνα ἡμῖν ὁ Θεὸς ἐπισιτισμὸν ἀποστείλῃ εἰς
πλησμονήν· οὐχ ὥστε γεύεσθαι μόνον, ἀλλὰ καὶ πληρωθῆναι τῶν λόγων τῆς ζωῆς,
καὶ ἰσχυροποιηθῆναι ἐν αὐτοῖς. Πλὴν ἡ προηγουμένη τροφὴ αὕτη ἐστίν. Ἐσθιόντων
δέ ποτε τὸ μάννα Ἑβραῖοι ἔλε γον· Οὐδὲν, πλὴν εἰς τὸ μάννα οἱ ὀφθαλμοὶ ἡμῶν.
Ἐμνήσθημεν γάρ, ὅτι ἐκαθέσθημεν ἐπὶ τῶν λεβή των τῶν κρεῶν ἐν Αἰγύπτῳ· καὶ
ἡμεῖς ταλανίζο μεν ἐκείνους, ὡς τότε ἡμαρτηκότας· οὐχ ὁρῶντες, ὅτι καὶ ἐν ἡμῖν
ταῦτα τὰ ἁμαρτήματα γίνεται· ἀντὶ τῆς πνευματικῆς Γραφῆς τὰ πράσα τὰ δυσώδη,
καὶ τὰ κρόμμυα τὰ βλάπτοντα τοὺς ὀφθαλμοὺς τῆς ψυ χῆς, καὶ τὰ πληροῦντα
δυσωδίαν ἁμαρτήματα σκό ροδα ἐπιθυμοῦμεν φαγεῖν, καὶ ἐμφορηθῆναι ἡδονῶν
δυσοσμίας. Καὶ τὴν ἔκλυτον τοῦ κόσμου καὶ τῶν σωματικῶν φύσιν ποθοῦντες,
πεπόνων ἐπιθυμοῦμεν, καὶ τὸ μὴ ἀναδιδόμενον εἰς τὴν τῆς ψυχῆς οὐσίαν ἀνελόντες,
σικύων θέλομεν μεταλαμβάνειν. Καὶ ἐπειδὴ οὐ θέλομεν τὸν ἄρτον, τὸν ἐκ τοῦ
οὐρανοῦ, οὗ προφῆται κήρυκες καὶ δίκαιοι, νεφέλαι καλούμενοι διὰ τὸ ὑψοῦ

If you wish, whatever we gather here in preparation, having rested there on the Sabbath, we shall find and be nourished. Long ago, then, God gave bread from heaven to His people, unable to be weary, sufficient for every pleasure; for whatever one desired, it was judged accordingly. Such is the nature of the word that nourishes the soul, changing according to the power of the one being nourished. If the law nourishes an infant, it becomes milk; if a weak soul, it becomes vegetable; if perfect, solid food. But the manna does not come to those sitting still, but to those going forth outside the camp; I speak indeed of the body, in which the soul is entrapped. For the soul must no longer be in flesh, but in spirit. And no one bearing the image of the earthly man is able to eat heavenly bread, because the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit. Concerning this food, you too were taught to pray. If then you take the daily bread, the one not withdrawing, the one not refusing, the one being given back into the substance of the soul, when I reason concerning God, concerning Christ, concerning His divinity, concerning His indwelling in human body and soul, I eat angels' bread, that is, the manna; having found and marveled at it, I shall speak wonderfully: Manna; what is this? pass_b_english: In the shadows of Moses, we seek the truth contained within them, drawing forth both new and old insights from the treasury of divine wisdom.
If you desire, whatever we gather here in preparation, having rested in that place on the Sabbath, we will discover there and be sustained by it.
Long ago, God provided bread from heaven to His people, a sustenance that never fails, fully sufficient for every delight, responding precisely to what each person desired.
Such is the nature of the word that nourishes the soul: it adapts its form according to the capacity of the one who receives it.
When the law feeds an infant, it becomes milk; when it feeds a weak soul, it becomes vegetables; when it feeds a perfect one, it becomes solid food.
Yet this manna does not come to those who remain idle, but to those who go forth outside the camp—I speak of the body, in which the soul is presently confined.
For the soul must no longer dwell in flesh, but in spirit.
No one who bears the image of the earthly man can partake of heavenly bread, because the natural person does not receive the things of the Spirit.
Regarding this food, you too were taught to pray.

Therefore, if you take the daily bread—the one that does not withdraw, does not refuse, but is continually given back into the substance of the soul—when I reflect on God, on Christ, on His divinity, on His indwelling in the human body and soul, I eat the bread of angels, that is, the manna.
Having found it and marveled at it, I will speak wonderfully: 'Manna—what is this?' And this utterance shall become the name of that bread.
Pray that God may send us provision for true satisfaction—not merely to taste, but also to be filled with the words of life, and to be strengthened by them.
Yet the preceding food is this very manna.
While eating the manna, the Hebrews said: 'Nothing, except that our eyes were directed toward the manna.'

We recalled that we had sat down by the meat pots in Egypt, and we accused those people of having sinned at that time, failing to recognize that the very same sins are taking place within ourselves; instead of turning to the spiritual Scripture, we crave to eat foul-smelling greens and onions that damage the soul’s sight, and we long to be filled with the pleasures that come from sinful, stinking indulgences.

And as we yearn for the cleansing of the world and the purification of our bodily nature, we thirst for hard labor, and having stripped away what does not contribute to the soul’s true substance, we desire to partake of cucumbers; furthermore, since we do not want the heavenly bread—of which prophets, heralds, and the righteous are spoken of as clouds due to their lofty stature—we turn instead to these earthly, corrupt desires.
